$comment: The qibla and the new moon section of the explorer (src/ui/explore/islamic-panel.ts): loaded with its chunk (I18n.extend). Its labels on the globe and the navigator’s title are in en.explore.json.
ui.universe.islamic.intro: Worked out from the Sun and the Moon with the explorer’s own ephemeris, for learning. For prayer, follow your local mosque; for the start of a month, your community’s practice.
ui.universe.islamic.noPlace: Come close to the Earth, or find a place, to see its qibla.
ui.universe.islamic.bearing: {degrees}° from true north ({compass}), {distance} to the Kaaba
ui.universe.islamic.showPath: Show the way on the globe
ui.universe.islamic.qiblaNote: The qibla here is the direction of the shortest path over the Earth to the Kaaba (a great circle), measured from true north. A compass points to magnetic north, which differs by the local magnetic declination.
ui.universe.islamic.sunIntro: Twice a year the Sun passes straight over the Kaaba at midday there. At that moment, wherever it is day, every upright shadow points straight away from the qibla. Twice more it passes over the point of the Earth opposite the Kaaba, and on that side of the world shadows point toward it.
ui.universe.islamic.prayerTitle: The Sun and the times of prayer
ui.universe.islamic.prayerIntro: The times of prayer follow the Sun: dawn and nightfall when it is a set depth below the horizon, midday when it crosses the meridian, the afternoon when a shadow reaches a set length. Communities set these depths and lengths differently; each published convention gives its own times.
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.convention.te: Institute of Geophysics, University of Tehran
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.convention.ru: Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Russia
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.asrNote: Asr begins when a shadow is longer than its noon shadow by its object’s length (the Shafi’i, Maliki, Hanbali and Ja’fari reckoning) or by twice it (the Hanafi).
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.for: At {place}, on {date} (its local day), in UTC:
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.fajr: Fajr: the Sun {deg}° below the horizon
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.dhuhr: Dhuhr: the Sun crosses the meridian, {alt}° high
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.maghribDeg: Maghrib: the Sun {deg}° below the horizon
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.ishaDeg: Isha: the Sun {deg}° below the horizon
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.ishaRamadan: Isha: {minutes} minutes after Maghrib, in Ramadan
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.none: None: the Sun does not go so far below the horizon this night
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.noSun: None: the Sun does not rise and set this day
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.note: Times are for sea level and to the minute, in UTC: the explorer knows no time zones. Timetables usually add a minute or more to Dhuhr for caution, and some add minutes to Maghrib. Where the Sun does not go so far below the horizon, as in summer far from the equator, communities use further conventions, which are not shown: the middle of the night, a seventh of the night, or a share by angle. For prayer, follow your community’s own timetable.
ui.universe.islamic.prayer.credit: Conventions as PrayTimes.org lists them (H. Zarrabi-Zadeh), each its institution’s.
ui.universe.islamic.astrolabe.title: An astrolabe for this place
ui.universe.islamic.astrolabe.intro: An astrolabe draws the sky flat by stereographic projection. On a plate made for one latitude lie the horizon, circles of equal altitude every 10° and lines of equal azimuth; over it turns the rete, with the stars and the Sun’s yearly path. The Science Museum in London keeps a brass astrolabe made in Syria between 901 and 1100, with plates for three latitudes; among its uses was telling the time.
ui.universe.islamic.astrolabe.how: This one is drawn for the place the qibla is reckoned from, at the time shown, with the stars the IAU names that are brighter than magnitude 2 on its rete. The rule, from the centre through the Sun, reads the local apparent time on the rim; the dashed circle lies 18° below the horizon, the Sun’s depression several of the conventions above use for Fajr or Isha. Let the time run and the rete turns once a sidereal day.
ui.universe.islamic.astrolabe.credit: The projection as Snyder gives it (Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS, 1987); the stars from the Bright Star Catalogue, named by the IAU; the astrolabe in London from the Science Museum Group’s catalogue (object 1981-1380).
ui.universe.islamic.astrolabe.label: An astrolabe’s plate for {lat}, its rete turned to the time shown with {count} named stars and the Sun
ui.universe.islamic.astrolabe.above: The Sun {alt}° above the horizon; the rule reads {time} local apparent time.
ui.universe.islamic.astrolabe.below: The Sun {alt}° below the horizon; the rule reads {time} local apparent time.
ui.universe.islamic.golden: Along its meridian, the Kaaba is {ratio} times as far from the South Pole as from the North Pole; the golden ratio is {golden}. The latitude that divides the meridian exactly in the golden ratio, {latitude}° N, runs {km} km south of the Kaaba ({kaaba}° N), measured on the WGS 84 ellipsoid. A closeness of numbers, shown at its actual size; it is not offered as evidence of anything.

ui.universe.islamic.mapNote: Yallop’s test (B. D. Yallop, NAO Technical Note 69, 1997) judges the crescent by the Moon’s height above the Sun and the crescent’s width at the best time to look, four ninths of the way from sunset to moonset. It describes what the sky allows, not when a month begins: communities begin each month by their own practice, by sighting, local or global, or by calculation.
ui.universe.islamic.mapNoteOdeh: Odeh’s test (M. Sh. Odeh, Experimental Astronomy 18, 2004) is drawn from 737 sightings and failed attempts, almost half of them by the Islamic Crescents’ Observation Project. It judges the crescent by the Moon’s height above the Sun and the crescent’s width as seen from the place itself, at the same best time to look. It describes what the sky allows, not when a month begins: communities begin each month by their own practice, by sighting, local or global, or by calculation.
ui.universe.islamic.heritage.title: Astronomers and geometers of the Islamic world
ui.universe.islamic.heritage.raqqa.name: Raqqa
ui.universe.islamic.heritage.raqqa.note: Al-Battani observed here from 877. He measured the length of the year as 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes and 24 seconds, a few minutes from today’s value.
ui.universe.islamic.heritage.isfahan.not: In his Book of Fixed Stars (964), written at the Buyid court, Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described a “little cloud” in Andromeda: the earliest known record of another galaxy. With the sky’s star names shown, the explorer names it at its place.
ui.universe.islamic.heritage.maragheh.no: The observatory founded in 1259 for Nasir al-Din al-Tusi; its tables of the Sun, the Moon and the planets (the Ilkhanic tables) were finished in 1272.
ui.universe.islamic.heritage.samarkand.n: Ulugh Beg’s observatory, built in the 1420s, with a great meridian arc cut into the hill; its star catalogue was made there. The arc was found again in 1908.
ui.universe.islamic.heritage.darb-i-imam: Its tiled portal (1453) is laid in girih patterns that Lu and Steinhardt (Science, 2007) read as nearly a Penrose tiling, a pattern whose proportions are set by the golden ratio; other scholars question how close the match is.
ui.universe.islamic.heritage.istanbul.no: Taqi al-Din’s observatory, among the largest of its age, was pulled down in 1580, a few years after it was built.
